Why New York generates ET demand

The New York market runs on infrastructure — power generation across the state, the harbour and its terminals, one of the world's largest transit systems, and the structural steel that a continuously rebuilding city consumes.

Condenser and feedwater heater tubing is eddy current's core power-generation work — full-bundle screening each major outage with plugging decisions made tube by tube.

Material verification and sorting — mixed stock, heat-treat condition checks — bring eddy current into fabrication QA alongside dedicated weld techniques.

Marine diesel engine components, turbocharger parts and shaft tapers are examined with eddy current during overhaul, where a missed crack ends up as a tow.

Rolling-contact fatigue on the railhead is screened with eddy current from inspection vehicles, complementing the ultrasonic programme.

What typically gets examined

In practice that means ET work across generating station pressure parts, bridge and building structural steel, port and terminal equipment, and subway and commuter rail infrastructure — with scope set by the damage mechanisms each asset actually runs, not by a standard menu.

Certification and acceptance in New York

New York State boiler law and NBIC govern statutory equipment; structural work on public projects carries AWS D1.1 CWI inspection requirements written into contract, and transit work follows the authorities' own engineering standards with night-possession scheduling.

Examinations themselves are performed to ASME Section V Article 8 and its tubing appendices, ISO 15548, and ASTM E243 for tube examination. The evidence chain — technician certification current on the day, instrument and reference block calibration, and the procedure revision in force — travels with every report, because that bundle is what an audit actually checks.
